title: Lineage-Aware Memory Governance: A Derivation-Gated Framework for Privacy-Preserving Column-Level Access Control in Enterprise AI Agents

object.carrier: Analytical Memory Unit (AMU) records in a shared cross-department agent memory store: tuple <metric_name, value, owner_dept, epoch, lineage L> where L is a sequence of (table, columns, filter) derivation steps, plus cached sensitive-column set S(a) and a 12-character SHA256 definition hash H(a)

safety_property.statement: Under complete lineage recording (Assumption 1), the lineage-gated retrieval policy never returns to a requesting department a cached result whose derivation touches a sensitive column outside that department's permitted column set (Theorem 1, a conditional design guarantee proved by construction). The guarantee degrades under incomplete lineage (measured leaks eliminated only at 75-90% recorded completeness, Experiment 3) and does not cover inference attacks through undeclared derived features (threat T4). Operationally judged by cross-department leak rate (0.0% vs naive 18.8-25.5%) at a reuse-rate cost, plus KPI definition-conflict recall.
safety_property.operationalized_as: leak rate (% of retrievals serving results whose ground-truth derivation touches blocked sensitive columns, measured against a shadow store with exact ground truth in a discrete-event simulator), memory reuse rate (%), conflict recall (%), and microsecond gate latency

capabilities: honest-but-potentially-over-privileged enterprise departments request metrics they have legitimate business need for, but not all derivation paths fall within their column permissions (the T1 leakage path requires no malice)
retrieval of cached results from the shared memory store across departments
(T5, partial) fabricating or under-reporting self-declared lineage when agents report lineage themselves
(T8, partial) prompt injection or timing side-channel targeting the lineage path
assumptions: Assumption 1 (complete lineage): every stored AMU's lineage records every table, column, and filter predicate of the computation that produced its value
source-layer column access control (e.g., Apache Ranger, Unity Catalog) is enforced for fresh queries; AMU governs only the memory layer
the fallback fresh computation is computed entirely within the requester's permissions (precondition of the retrieval algorithm)
the gate reasons about one retrieval at a time; no collusion or out-of-band sharing of individually safe results between departments
not_covered: T4: inference attacks via derived features that encode sensitive information without naming the source column (called the most consequential gap for production use)
T6: aggregate inference across multiple retrievals, including cross-metric correlation triangulating a denied column
T7: insider threats on the memory store itself (delegated to trusted infrastructure and audit logging)
departmental collusion reconstructing a sensitive derivation from disjoint individually safe cached results
non-SQL derivations (vector stores, REST/GraphQL, in-process) beyond the SQL lineage extractor exercised

intervention.name: Analytical Memory Unit (AMU) schema with lineage-gated retrieval policy and definition-hash conflict detection
intervention.description: Every cached analytical result stores its full derivation (lineage) graph of (table, columns, filter) steps plus two cached quantities: the sensitive-column set S(a) (union of accessed columns intersected with the sensitive registry) and a SHA256-based definition hash H(a). At retrieval, a gate serves a memory hit only if S(a) is a subset of the requester department's permitted columns P(d) (O(n) worst case, most-recent-first scan); otherwise the agent falls back to a fresh in-scope computation that is itself written back. The write path compares H(a) across departments to surface silent same-named-KPI definition drift without blocking writes. The design fails closed (extraction failure marks the AMU maximally sensitive; unavailable permission set defaults to denial), and the epoch field supports TTL eviction and policy-driven invalidation with lazy S(a) recomputation after policy updates (Corollary 3). Automatic SQL lineage extraction (SQLGlot at the database cursor) removes reliance on agent self-reporting.

controls.name: Naive Shared Memory (content-gated, representing prior systems such as MemGPT/Zep/A-MEM)
Synthetic 5-table schema vs TPC-H 8-table schema (sensitive registry size 3 vs 9)
Conflict detectors D1 (exact hash) / D2 (Jaccard) / D3 (column-graph) on the same 43 pairs

results.claim: In the simulator, naive content-gated shared memory structurally leaks sensitive derivations cross-department (18.8% synthetic, 25.5% TPC-H), while the lineage-aware system shows 0.0% leaks in both schemas - the 0.0% being a consequence of the Theorem 1 guarantee in the setting tested, with the non-zero naive baseline as the empirical content.
results.setting: pure-Python discrete-event simulator isolating retrieval from LLM/network confounds; 5-table synthetic schema (|S|=3) and 8-table TPC-H (|S|=9); 30 seeds each, mean ± std, bootstrap 95% CI excludes zero, Mann-Whitney U p<0.001

results.claim: The protection costs a 13-14 percentage-point memory-reuse reduction (roughly 13 additional query executions per 100 requests), i.e., lineage-aware retrieval keeps 82.6% (synthetic) and 81.5% (TPC-H) of the reuse that naive content-gated memory provides (95.8%).
results.setting: same simulator comparison of Naive Shared Memory vs Lineage-Aware, 30 seeds per schema, two schemas (synthetic 5-table, TPC-H 8-table)

denominator.how_counted: per-request basis in the simulator workload; §VI-A describes the cost as 'roughly 13 additional query executions per 100 requests'

results.claim: The definition-hash conflict detector catches all cross-department KPI definition conflicts (recall 100.0%) where the naive baseline catches none (0.0%), on both schemas.
results.setting: same simulator comparison, 30 seeds per schema (synthetic 5-table and TPC-H 8-table)

results.claim: The safety guarantee degrades with lineage completeness: at rho=0.50 truncated lineage gives almost no protection (16.3% synthetic, 10.3% TPC-H leak), while measured leaks reach 0% only at rho>=0.75 (synthetic) or rho>=0.90 (TPC-H), motivating the recommended rho>=0.9 deployment target.
results.setting: completeness rho defined as fraction of each step's columns correctly reported; true leak rate measured via shadow store with ground-truth sensitivity; 30 seeds, both schemas (Experiment 3)
results.quote:
At ρ=0.50\rho{=}0.50, truncated lineage gives almost no protection (synthetic:
16.3±3.3%16.3\pm 3.3\% leak; TPC-H: 10.3±4.7%10.3\pm 4.7\%). At ρ≥0.75\rho\geq 0.75 (synthetic)

results.claim: On 43 hand-labelled lineage pairs, no single fuzzy conflict detector is production-ready: exact-hash D1 catches everything (recall 1.000, all 8/8 logic-operator changes) with weak precision 0.651, while column-graph D3 has perfect precision 1.000 but recall 0.714 (F1 0.833), missing all logic-operator changes (0/8).
results.value: D1: precision 0.651, recall 1.000, F1 0.789, LO 8/8; D3: precision 1.000, recall 0.714, F1 0.833, LO 0/8
results.setting: 43 hand-labelled lineage pairs: 15 true conflicts, 15 threshold variants, 8 logic-operator (AND->OR) changes, 5 column-subset cases; detectors D1 exact hash, D2 Jaccard (tau=0.70), D3 column-graph (Experiment 4)

results.claim: Gating overhead is negligible: worst-case retrieve latency scales linearly from 0.66 microseconds at n=1 to 13.82 microseconds at n=50 (a 21x increase confirming O(n)), while expected-case and conflict-detection paths stay flat (O(1)).
results.setting: time.perf_counter() over 2,000 iterations at five store sizes n in {1,5,10,20,50}; single-threaded CPython 3.10.12 in Docker on a 4-core Apple Silicon ARM64 VM, 3.8 GB RAM, Ubuntu 22.04, no GPU/SIMD/JIT (Experiment 5)

results.claim: In a real-agent proof-of-concept with automatic sqlglot lineage extraction (Northwind, LangChain+Ollama), zero sensitive-column leaks occurred across all 9 cross-department round-trips, and both gate blocks coincided with the 2 automatically detected metric-definition conflicts (no false positives) - a feasibility demonstration, not evidence of production viability.
results.value: zero leaks / 9 round-trips; 2 gate blocks coincided with 2 detected conflicts; 4 requests served from cache
results.setting: Northwind database, 4 departments (Finance, Sales, Operations, HR), sensitive registry {unitprice, freight, homephone, birthdate}, LangChain+Ollama agent issuing real (and demo-mode canned) SQL across three scenarios; sqlglot AST-based automatic lineage extraction interposed at the database cursor (Experiment 6)
results.quote:
Across all 9 cross-department round-trips, zero sensitive-column leaks
occur: 5 fresh SQL queries are executed and written (2 following a gate
block), 4 requests are served entirely from cache, and 2 gate blocks
precisely coincide with the 2 automatically detected metric-definition

denominator.how_counted: across three scenarios covering safe reuse, blocked-with-conflict, and vacuous reuse on a metric with no sensitive columns (§VI-E)

limitations.statement: The headline naive leak rates (18.8-25.5%) are properties of the authors' specific workload mixes, not universal base rates, though the authors argue the structural leakage argument holds regardless of the specific percentage.
limitations.quote:

limitations.statement: The mechanism does not catch inference attacks that encode sensitive information in a derived feature without naming the source column (threat T4), which the authors call the most important gap for production use.

limitations.statement: The 43-pair fuzzy conflict-detection dataset is still small, and the runtime benchmarks were measured on a single hardware/OS configuration so the reported constants (though not the O(n)-vs-O(1) scaling) may shift on other platforms.

limitations.statement: The zero-leak result of the real-agent experiment has a completeness gap: a purely syntactic SQL extractor cannot resolve views, stored procedures, and deep aliasing, so closing Assumption 1 fully needs catalog-aware view/procedure expansion left as future work.
limitations.quote:
Experiment 6’s zero-leak result that a purely syntactic extractor cannot
close on its own; closing it needs catalog-aware view/procedure expansion,
which we flag as future work rather than something the current
implementation already does.

limitations.statement: The real-agent study is explicitly a nine-round-trip feasibility demonstration, not evidence of production viability.
limitations.quote:
real-agent proof-of-concept with LLM-generated SQL is consistent with the
guarantee: zero leaks over 9 round-trips, two conflicts caught
automatically – though a feasibility demonstration, not evidence of
production viability.

reproduction.code: Reference implementation (AMU/lineage data model, three competing memory systems, event-replay simulator, statistical analysis, sqlglot-based real-agent pipeline) containerised via Docker Compose; to be released in a public repository upon acceptance, available from the corresponding author on request in the interim (§VIII)
reproduction.data: Generated synthetic and TPC-H-inspired benchmark data plus the public fictional Northwind database; no proprietary or personal data (§VIII)
